_comment: Integration test cases for HelFEM. This file is DATA -- edit it freely;
the runner (run_tests.py) is independent of what is listed here.
2. quick s-only systems (H, He, H2) and harder ones with p/pi orbitals
(Ne, Ar, Kr, BH, CH, NH, OH, FH, N2, CO)
4. HF, LDA, GGA, mGGA (tau- and laplacian-dependent) and hybrids
Bases are deliberately SMALL and FIXED. A regression test needs a
reproducible basis, not a converged one -- physical accuracy is a
separate concern. Diatomic grids were nonetheless derived with
diatomic_cbasis (see tools/gen_diatomic_grids.sh) so they are sane.
Determinism: every case runs with OMP_NUM_THREADS=1. Converged energies
are a deterministic function of the thread count (see the memory note
energies-depend-on-thread-count), so the thread count is part of the

cases._why: Runs 30 first-order iterations and then hands over to the second-order optimizer, which is how gensap should be driven: the spherically averaged atom optimizes its occupations as well as its orbitals, and first order handles a fractionally occupied degenerate shell badly. cases.name: diatomic-Ne-dummy-hf-absm
cases._why: Ne (2p^6) through the diatomic code at --symmetry=3. The p shell fills m=-1,0,+1, so the |m| blocks carry a real two-fold degeneracy, but the shell is closed and nothing breaks the symmetry -- so this must reproduce the per-m answer exactly. HF makes it the test of the exchange +-m mirror, which is only armed at --symmetry=3.

cases.name: diatomic-Ne-dummy-lda-absm
cases._why: As diatomic-Ne-dummy-hf-absm, but LDA: exercises the pure-m XC grid's +-m mirror rather than the exchange one.

cases.name: diatomic-H2-absm-hf
cases._why: H2 has only m=0, so --symmetry=3 collapses to a single block with degeneracy 1 and no mirror at all. Cheap guard on the plumbing -- block metadata, |m| labels, density scatter -- along the path where the degeneracy machinery must be a no-op.

cases.name: diatomic-CH-absm-hf
cases._why: CH (2-Pi) at --symmetry=3. The odd pi electron cannot sit wholly in +1 or -1 here: the degeneracy is folded into the block's maximum occupation, so it comes out as 0.5 in each -- the cylindrically averaged state. This is the case the retired --maverage could not converge at all (it constrained the Fock matrix but not the occupations, and stalled with the DIIS error pinned at 1.8e-5). The recorded energy is therefore ABOVE the symmetry-broken CH solutions, and the point of the test is that it converges.

cases.name: diatomic-NH-hf-absm
cases._why: NH (3-Sigma-) puts one pi electron in each of +-1, so its density IS symmetric under m -> -m and --symmetry=3 must reproduce the per-m answer exactly. Unlike Ne this is spin-polarised and open-shell, so it exercises the unrestricted path.

cases.name: diatomic-NH-lda-absm
cases._why: As diatomic-NH-hf-absm through the XC grid: the unrestricted pure-m density evaluation with an occupied pi shell.

cases.name: diatomic-CH-lda-absm
cases._why: CH (2-Pi) at --symmetry=3 through the XC grid. Companion to diatomic-CH-absm-hf; the recorded energy is the cylindrically averaged state and is NOT comparable to the pinned pi+/pi- ones.

cases.name: diatomic-Ne-dummy-gga-absm
cases._why: The LDA symmetry=3 cases exercise none of the gradient machinery. This one covers the shared gradient pass in the pure-m density evaluation, where a mirrored pair's contribution is taken once and weighted instead of walking both blocks.

cases.name: diatomic-Ne-dummy-mgga-absm
cases._why: Covers the tau and Laplacian passes, which build two further (nbf x nbf) x (nbf x nang) products per block (Pblk * dr_m and Pblk * dth_m) and are the dominant meta-GGA cost. Those are shared between mirrored partners, so an error there would show up here and nowhere else in the quick tier.

cases.name: aij-Fe-firstorder
cases._why: spin-restricted Fe: 4s and 3d come out degenerate and fractionally occupied, which is the case the first-order methods handle worst. ODA alone does not converge it in 2000 iterations. Paired with the second-order run below.

cases.name: aij-Fe-secondorder
cases._why: the same Fe atom through the trust-region optimizer, which optimizes the 4s/3d occupation transfer explicitly rather than waiting for the first-order iteration to find it.

cases.name: aij-Al-jellium-secondorder
cases._why: unrestricted second-order path: alpha and beta are separate particle types with separately conserved electron counts, which the restricted Fe pair does not exercise.

cases.name: gensap-Fe-secondorder
cases._why: spin-restricted Fe through the trust-region optimizer. This is the case that motivates the feature in gensap: the first-order solver does not converge here at all, and stops 0.103 Eh above the minimum, because 4s and 3d come out degenerate in different l blocks and no orbital rotation connects them. Matched to aij's bare-atom settings (lmax 4, core guess) so the two drivers can be compared directly.

cases.name: gensap-Fe-hf-firstorder
cases._why: spin-polarized Fe at Hartree-Fock, where the Fock matrix carries exact exchange. Paired with the second-order run below: exchange is the one term of the response the DFT cases never exercise. Deliberately left at first order when the rest of the gensap cases were switched over: it is the reference half of gensap-secondorder-equals-firstorder-Fe-hf, and without it nothing here would compare the two paths directly.

cases.name: gensap-Fe-hf-secondorder
cases._why: the same Hartree-Fock atom through the trust-region optimizer, so that the analytic exchange response is tied to the ordinary SCF.

invariants.name: Be-field-Ez-sign-degeneracy
invariants._why: an atom in a uniform electric field is reflection symmetric, so +field and -field must be EXACTLY degenerate

invariants.name: Be-field-Bz-sign-degeneracy
invariants._why: with m-symmetric occupations the Zeeman term cancels under B -> -B, so +field and -field must be EXACTLY degenerate

invariants.name: Be-unoccupied-p-does-not-contribute
invariants._why: an angular momentum present in the basis but unoccupied must not change the energy: lmax=0 and pinned-lmax=2 must agree. Measured -14.5450377121 for both, bit-for-bit. Catches the p basis leaking into the density.

invariants.name: H2-purem-fast-path-equals-general-path
invariants._why: the pure-m path is an exact restriction, not an approximation: with a cylindrically symmetric density only M=0 survives, so dropping the phi quadrature changes nothing. Measured identical at every SCF iteration, -1.1374807779 both ways, at 4.74s vs 68.87s (14.5x). This guards the fast path against silently diverging from the general one.

invariants.name: aij-njellium0-equals-bare-atom
invariants._why: with no jellium electrons the atom-in-jellium problem IS the bare atom, so aij must reproduce the plain spherical solver exactly. Measured -240.3560448251 from both, to all printed digits. Ties the jellium machinery to the plain solvers at the one point where the two must coincide, with no reference values involved. (gensap carries an unoccupied d shell that aij does not; that it changes nothing is the same fact as the Be unoccupied-p invariant.)

invariants.name: diatomic-with-dummy-equals-atomic-He
invariants._why: a zero-charge centre adds no physics, so the diatomic code must reproduce the atomic one. Unlike gensap-equals-atomic this is convergence-limited rather than an identity -- the two use entirely different bases (prolate spheroidal vs radial x spherical harmonics) -- but with a cbasis-derived grid the agreement is sub-nanohartree: -2.8616799948 against -2.8616799946, and the tighter bases on each side converge to within 2e-10. Exercises the prolate spheroidal machinery -- Legendre expansion, off-centre nuclear attraction, the 2D basis -- against a known atomic answer.

invariants.name: H2-purem-equals-general-gga
invariants._why: the pure-m path is an exact restriction: with a cylindrically symmetric density only M=0 survives, so dropping the phi quadrature changes nothing. Measured -1.1666914700 for both paths, speedup 91.6x (733s vs 8s). The general path is exercised by no other test and by no default run (purem is auto-on whenever symmetry>=1), so without this a divergence could persist indefinitely.

invariants.name: H2-purem-equals-general-mgga
invariants._why: the pure-m path is an exact restriction: with a cylindrically symmetric density only M=0 survives, so dropping the phi quadrature changes nothing. Measured -1.1804586903 for both paths, speedup 139x (3477s vs 25s). The general path is exercised by no other test and by no default run (purem is auto-on whenever symmetry>=1), so without this a divergence could persist indefinitely.

invariants.name: Be-field-Ez-sign-degeneracy-lda
invariants._why: degeneracy on the DFT path, which is where it can actually break: the XC energy is a numerical quadrature, so a grid not symmetric under z -> -z would break the degeneracy here and nowhere else. At HF the exchange is analytic and the symmetry holds by construction.

invariants.name: Be-field-Bz-sign-degeneracy-lda
invariants._why: degeneracy on the DFT path, which is where it can actually break: the XC energy is a numerical quadrature, so a grid not symmetric under m -> -m would break the degeneracy here and nowhere else. At HF the exchange is analytic and the symmetry holds by construction.

invariants.name: Be-field-Ez-sign-degeneracy-gga

invariants.name: Be-field-Bz-sign-degeneracy-gga

invariants.name: CH-pi-plus-equals-minus-hf
invariants._why: pi+ and pi- are related by reflection, so they must be EXACTLY degenerate -- the molecular analogue of the O 3P p+/p- check. The HF variant is the one that can actually break: the XC energy is a numerical quadrature, so a grid not symmetric under m -> -m would break the degeneracy there and nowhere else.

invariants.name: absm-equals-perm-Ne-hf
invariants._why: A closed p shell is symmetric under m -> -m, so solving one block per |m| with the degeneracy in max_occ must land on the same solution as solving every m separately. Measured 3e-10 apart.

invariants.name: absm-equals-perm-Ne-lda
invariants._why: As absm-equals-perm-Ne-hf, through the XC grid instead of exchange. Measured identical to all printed digits.

invariants.name: absm-equals-perm-H2
invariants._why: With only m=0 present the |m| grouping is the identity, so the two must agree exactly; any drift means the degeneracy or the mirrored scatter is firing where it should not.

invariants.name: absm-equals-perm-NH-hf
invariants._why: NH's pi shell is singly occupied in EACH of +-1, so the density is already m -> -m symmetric and constraining it changes nothing. The energies must agree; if they do not, the |m| solver is not reproducing the state it claims to.

invariants.name: absm-equals-perm-NH-lda
invariants._why: As absm-equals-perm-NH-hf, through the XC grid.

invariants.name: absm-equals-perm-Ne-gga
invariants._why: Closed p shell: grouping the m blocks must not change the answer. Measured identical to all printed digits.

invariants.name: absm-equals-perm-Ne-mgga
invariants._why: As absm-equals-perm-Ne-gga, through the tau/Laplacian passes.

invariants.name: aij-secondorder-equals-firstorder-Fe
invariants._why: the second-order optimizer must find the SAME minimum as the first-order one, not merely a fast one. Reference-free: it ties the trust-region path, its analytic gradient and its XC response kernel to the ordinary SCF at the point where the two must agree. Fe is the case where they disagree most easily, since the 4s/3d occupations are free parameters and a wrong occupation Hessian lands on a different stationary point with a plausible-looking energy.

invariants.name: aij-secondorder-equals-firstorder-Al-jellium
invariants._why: same statement for the unrestricted path, where the occupation transfers are confined within a spin.

invariants.name: gensap-secondorder-equals-aij-bare-atom-Fe
invariants._why: aij with no jellium IS the bare atom, so gensap's second-order path and aij's must land on the same number. Reference-free, and it crosses two independent drivers: the energy expressions, the Fock builders and the SCF drivers are separate code, and only the trust-region optimizer beneath them is shared. Fe is the case that discriminates, since the 4s/3d occupations are free parameters and a wrong occupation Hessian lands on a different stationary point with a plausible-looking energy -- which is exactly what the first-order solver does here, 0.103 Eh high.

invariants.name: gensap-secondorder-equals-firstorder-Fe-hf
invariants._why: the second-order optimizer must find the same minimum as the ordinary SCF when the Fock matrix carries exact exchange. Exchange is linear in the density, so its response is exact -- but it is a separate term from the Coulomb and XC ones, and nothing else in the suite exercises it through the Hessian.
